extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, administrative law students, policymakers and practitioners working with Canadian social security/administrative tribunals
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed descriptive analysis of the Pension Appeals Board (PAB), related pension and unemployment-insurance legislation, and the administrative organization and appeal procedures that govern contributions and benefits. Focuses on statutory titles, delegated functions, appeal routes, tribunal composition, and consequences for administrative procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parent legislation must set out substantive provisions and decision-making process (initial and appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: As pieces of legislation, the two pension plans are largely similar in conception. In each case, the parent legislation contains the essential substantive provisions of the plan as well as a description of the decision-making process both in its initial phase and at the level of appeals against initial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parent statute should include both substantive rules (eligibility, contribution/benefit formulas, offences, etc.) and a description of administrative decision-making and available avenues of appeal; further procedural detail may be delegated to regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quebec Pension Plan structure (seven Titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The QPP contains seven titles: Title One (Definitions and application); Title Two (Quebec Pension Board); Title Three (Contributions); Title Four (Benefits); Title Five (Review); Title Six (Administration); Title Seven (Final provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each Title has a focused remit: definitions and applicability; creation and powers of the Board; rules for calculating/collecting/reimbursing contributions and related offences; eligibility criteria, benefit calculations, and payment conditions; recourse/appeal processes; administrative supports, confidentiality, delegated regulation-making and offences; coordination with social aid. When analyzing or drafting pension legislation, mirror this division to separate definitional, substantive, procedural and administrative matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal routes under the QPP: distinct avenues for contributions and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The QPP envisages two distinct avenues of recourse, one in matters of contributions and the other in matters of benefits. For contributions, appeals are lodged directly with the Review Commission; for benefits there are two levels of review: first before the Quebec Pension Board itself (hierarchical review) and then before the Review Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design litigation routes carefully: contributions disputes may be handled directly by a Review Commission while benefits disputes may require an internal/exhaustive first-level review before external appeal. The arrangement affects parties' procedural strategy and tribunal workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 193 (QPP) removes Review Commission jurisdiction over self-employed contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 193 — like its counterpart in the CPP, section 37 — removes from the jurisdiction of the Review Commission litigation connected with contributions by self-employed individuals, and assigns it to that of the fiscal authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory carve-outs can reassign disputes (e.g., self-employed contribution disputes) from tribunal review to fiscal authorities; check counterpart provisions in related statutes to determine jurisdictional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation respecting benefits governs pre-decision procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Like the CPP, the QPP is completed by a regulation of extensive scope, the Regulation respecting benefits. It is almost entirely devoted to the procedure to be followed in treating applications for benefits prior to the first decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that detailed application-processing steps (what happens before the first administrative decision) will be set out in subordinate instruments (regulations); substantive statutes may leave these procedural specifics to regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal/regimental instruments may govern Board review procedures (Reglement de regie interne)
rubrics_metrics.description: An unpublished instrument entitled Reglement de regie interne de la Regie des rentes du Quebec contains a portion that deals with the review of decisions before the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative bodies may adopt internal rules (possibly unpublished) governing internal review; analysts should review both public statutes/regulations and internal instruments to understand full procedure before a Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure before the Review Commission differs for contributions and benefits (two distinct regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: As in federal practice, the procedure used in Quebec before the Review Commission is the subject of two distinct regulations, depending upon whether the litigation concerns contributions or benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate procedural regimes for different subject-matters are common; when preparing or evaluating appeals, identify which regulatory regime applies (contributions vs benefits) since procedural requirements and timelines may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orders-in-Council can designate review tribunal and set financing/cost-sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Two Orders-in-Council by the Quebec Cabinet were made: one, under section 229 of the QPP, designates the PAB as the Review Commission of the Quebec plan; the second, dealing with the financing of the PAB, determines the mode of cost-sharing between the federal and the Quebec governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive instruments (Orders-in-Council) may be used to allocate jurisdictional functions (designating a tribunal) and to settle administrative arrangements such as cost-sharing. These instruments should be reviewed for their practical impact on tribunal jurisdiction and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unemployment Insurance Act: Parts III and IV govern contributions and collection, and provide appeal route (Umpire then PAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unemployment Insurance Act's Part III ('Contributions') and Part IV ('Collection of contributions') govern the calculation and collection of contributions and lay down administrative procedure leading to initial decisions and the appeal process: first to the unemployment insurance Umpire, and second to the PAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For unemployment insurance contribution disputes, identify the statutory parts and delegated procedural rules; appeals typically follow a first-instance administrative umpire and a second-level tribunal (PAB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unemployment Insurance Regulations specify insurable employment, contribution reductions and administrative procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act (Unemployment Insurance Regulations) treat contributions and related administrative procedure in Part I ('General'), Part III ('Insurable and excepted employment'), and Part IV ('Reduction of employer's premium').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed technical and procedural aspects of unemployment insurance contribution treatment are normally in the regulations; practitioners should consult relevant regulatory parts for definitional and procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: A particular regulation governs first-level appeals to the Umpire; no regulation for second-level appeals to PAB (UI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure applicable to the first level of contentious review (appeals to the Umpire) is the subject of a particular regulation. By contrast to the first level of appeal, no procedure has been laid down for second-level appeals to the PAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of regulatory procedure for a higher-level appeal creates procedural uncertainty and may shift reliance to tribunal practice or general administrative procedural principles; evaluate consequences for litigants (notice, evidence, timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of single comprehensive statute for PAB leads to dispersal of procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of a statute devoted exclusively to the constitution of this administrative tribunal and to a definition of its various powers has brought about a dispersal of its rules of procedure. The jurisdiction presently exercised by the PAB shows traces of its historical evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where tribunal powers/procedures are scattered across multiple statutes, regulations and orders, practitioners must aggregate sources to understand practice; such dispersal may produce apparent improvised or ad hoc procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal nature of contributory pensions: courts tend to treat benefits as private (insurance-like) for tort-damage assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have come increasingly to regard social insurance benefits as private. The Supreme Court of Canada declared it improper to take into account benefits received under a contributory pension plan in assessing damages from a work accident, assimilating the plan to a private insurance contract (i.e., not deductible from tort damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judicial characterization of pensions (public service vs private insurance) has concrete legal effects—e.g., whether benefits reduce tort damages. When litigating or drafting policy, be aware of precedent and possible legislative exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of functional specialization in administrative organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The system is dominated by the idea of specialization: the performance of functions (collection of contributions, distribution of benefits, investment of surplus funds, settlement of litigation) is entrusted to administrative authorities specialized in operations of that type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures commonly assign distinct functions to different agencies (tax collection, benefits administration, investment funds, adjudication). This affects coordination, accountability, and appeals; analysis of administrative procedure must consider which specialized body performed the initial act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of CPP functions to specific federal departments and agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In the CPP: Department of National Revenue collects contributions; Department of National Health and Welfare allocates and pays benefits; Department of Employment and Immigration assigns social insurance numbers; Department of Finance manages accounts and investments; Pension Appeals Board settles litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or appealing CPP-related decisions, identify which department performed the contested function since that determines record sources, applicable procedures, and institutional knowledge; statutes may integrate tasks into existing departmental machinery for efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of QPP functions to Quebec agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In the QPP: Quebec Department of Revenue determines and collects contributions; Quebec Pension Board allocates and pays benefits and may also administer other provincial social benefits; Quebec Deposit and Investment Fund manages collection surpluses and investment policy; litigation jurisdiction has been shared between the PAB (contributions) and the Social Affairs Commission (benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provincial arrangements may mirror federal ones but with differing degrees of decentralization; practical effects include different administrative records, internal review practices, and institutional expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative organization for unemployment insurance mirrors pension plans but shifted over time
rubrics_metrics.description: With minor exceptions, the administrative organization of unemployment insurance shares functional specialization: contributions withheld by Department of National Revenue; allocation of benefits by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission; litigation concerning contributions to Umpire then PAB. Over time, functions have shifted (centralization of contributions collection to National Revenue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical shifts (centralization vs decentralization) affect current procedural arrangements and who is responsible for initial decisions; practitioners should be alert to reforms that move administrative functions between departments or agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization vs decentralization is a deliberate legislative choice affecting procedure and control
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal and Quebec legislatures both adopted functional specialization but made divergent choices on centralization: CPP chose near-complete centralization (operations entrusted to government departments except adjudication), while QPP chose near-total decentralization (most operations assigned to autonomous agencies except collection). These choices influence ministerial/parliamentary control and proximity to political power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational form (centralized departments vs autonomous agencies) changes procedural climate, visibility, political oversight, and potential independence of decisions; this is relevant when evaluating administrative fairness, accountability, and reform proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and appointment criteria of the PAB
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 85(2) of the CPP summarily defines PAB composition: membership was originally 3 to 6 persons with the Chairman appointed by Governor in Council from judges of the Exchequer Court (now Federal Court) or provincial superior courts; other members could be judges of district/county courts. A 1974 amendment created a Vice-Chairman and increased membership to a maximum of ten persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal composition rules (statutory caps, judicial eligibility for leadership posts) are important for independence, expertise, and legitimacy. When engaging with the PAB, practitioners should note statutory appointment qualifications and any recent amendments that change membership size or qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice-Chairman requirement: judicial background
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice-Chairman must be chosen from among the judges of the Federal Court or of the superior courts of the provinces (post created in 1974).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership offices may be statutorily constrained to persons with judicial experience; this influences tribunal governance and the legal background brought to adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational characteristics of the PAB (low profile, sporadic sittings, non-permanent members)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB carries on its activity in a deliberately low-key manner. Its hearings attract only those directly concerned; the PAB sits at irregular intervals and fairly infrequently; its members are not permanently on duty and do not reside near its seat of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical access considerations (infrequency of sittings, member availability) affect scheduling, timely review, and litigant expectations; procedural planners should account for the tribunal's low-frequency operation when advising clients or designing case strategies.
